intro: Families around the world eat different foods. They wear different clothes. They say hello in different words. They keep different holidays. In this unit, you will visit many of them.
You will meet rice, tortillas, bread and injera. You will see a kimono, a sari and a huipil. You will learn hola, bonjour, ni hao and namaste.
By the end, you can name customs from many places. You can ask a friend kind questions about home. You can say hello and thank you in new words.
bigQuestion: How do food, clothes, words and holidays make each family special?

timeline.t: We share bread from home and learn its name.
We try eating with chopsticks, a fork and the hand.
We look at clothes for hot and cold places.
We see special clothes for special days.
We learn to try new food kindly.
We say hello in four languages and learn a bow.
We learn about holidays families keep.
We make a class chart of thank-you words.

test.why: Ni hao is hello in Mandarin Chinese.

write.prompt: Why is it good to learn about other families' food, clothes, words and holidays? Tell your answer. Use two things you learned in this unit.

title: Food, Clothes, Words and Holidays

chapters.title: What's for Lunch Around the World?
chapters.bigQuestion: How do food and clothes show where a family comes from?

story.title: Five Kinds of Bread
story.kicker: One lunch table holds bread from five places.
paragraphs: It is lunch time in Room 12. Ms. Ruiz says, "Today we share bread from home." Each child opens a lunch box. Everyone looks at the table.
Mateo has a warm corn tortilla. Lina has soft, flat injera. It has tiny holes like a sponge. Ben has a long French bread. Priya has round naan. Mei has a white steamed bun.
The children take small bites. Mateo tries the steamed bun. "It is soft like a pillow!" he says. Lina shows how to tear injera with her fingers.
Ms. Ruiz smiles. "Five breads, five families," she says. "Every one is made with care." The children say thank you to each other.
story.think: What bread or food does your family make or eat a lot? How would you share it?

lessons.title: Rice and Tortillas
lessons.mainIdea: Many families in Asia eat rice, and many families in Mexico eat corn tortillas.
reading: Rice is a small grain. It grows in wet fields. Many families in China, India and Japan eat rice every day.
In Mexico, many families eat *tortillas*. A tortilla is a flat, round bread. It is made from corn. People fill tortillas with beans, meat or cheese.
Rice and tortillas are *staple foods*. A staple food is a food people eat again and again. It helps fill you up.

words.d: a flat, round bread made from corn or wheat
a main food that people eat very often

look.title: Food for Everyone
look.text: Every person has a right to enough food and clothes to stay healthy.
look.cite: United Nations, Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 25, 1948 (simple words)
look.prompt: Why do you think food and clothes are on this list?

check.q: What is a tortilla made from in Mexico?
check.why: The reading says a tortilla in Mexico is made from corn.

check.q: Where do many families eat rice every day?
check.why: The reading names China, India and Japan as places where many families eat rice.

check.q: What is a staple food?
choices: a food for one party only
a main food people eat again and again
check.why: A staple food is a main food people eat very often.

lessons.title: Bread and Injera
lessons.mainIdea: Many families in Europe eat bread, and many families in Ethiopia eat injera.
reading: Bread is made from wheat flour and water. In France, a long bread is called a baguette. In Germany, many families eat dark rye bread.
In Ethiopia, many families eat *injera*. Injera is a big, soft, flat bread. It is made from a tiny grain called *teff*. It tastes a little sour.
Food goes right on top of the injera. People tear off a piece. They use it to scoop up the food.

words.d: a soft, flat bread from Ethiopia with tiny holes
a tiny grain used to make injera

look.title: A Big Round Plate
look.text: Look at a big round injera on a tray. Red lentils sit on one side. Green beans sit on the other side. Two friends tear off pieces. They scoop up the food together.
look.prompt: How is injera like a plate and a spoon at the same time?

check.q: What grain is injera made from?
check.why: The reading says injera is made from a tiny grain called teff.

check.q: What is a long French bread called?
check.why: The reading says a long bread in France is called a baguette.

check.q: How do people eat food on injera?
choices: They tear off a piece and scoop the food.
They cook it in soup first.
check.why: People tear off a piece of injera and use it to scoop up the food.

lessons.title: Chopsticks and Forks
lessons.mainIdea: Many people in East Asia eat with chopsticks, and many people in Europe eat with forks.
reading: *Chopsticks* are two thin sticks. You hold them in one hand. Many families in China, Japan, Korea and Vietnam use them.
A *fork* has sharp points. Many families in Europe and the Americas eat with a fork and a knife.
Both tools help people pick up food. Chopsticks pinch the food. A fork pokes the food. Each one takes practice.

words.d: two thin sticks held in one hand to pick up food
an eating tool with points that pokes food

look.title: Two Bowls of Noodles
look.text: Look at two bowls of noodles. One girl lifts her noodles with chopsticks. One boy twirls his noodles on a fork. Both of them are smiling. Both of them are eating.
look.prompt: Which tool would you like to try? What would help you learn it?

check.q: How do chopsticks pick up food?
choices: They scoop it like a cup.
check.why: The reading says chopsticks pinch the food.

check.q: Which place is one where many families use chopsticks?
check.why: The reading names China, Japan, Korea and Vietnam.

check.q: What do chopsticks and forks both do?
choices: They help people pick up food.
check.why: Both are tools that help people pick up food.

lessons.title: Eating With the Hand
lessons.mainIdea: In many places, people eat with the right hand, and it is polite and clean.
reading: In India, Ethiopia and many other places, people often eat with the hand. They use the right hand. They wash their hands first.
The fingers mix rice and sauce into a small bite. Many people say food tastes better this way. It is a *custom*. A custom is a way a group does things for a long time.
Every custom has *manners*. Manners are kind ways to act. At many tables, you wait for others to start.

words.d: a way a group of people has done something for a long time
kind and polite ways to act with other people

look.title: Wash, Then Eat
look.text: Look at a family in India. Each person washes at the sink. They sit down. A plate of rice and dal sits in front of them. Grandma takes the first bite with her right hand.
look.prompt: What did this family do before eating? Why is that a good idea?

check.q: What do people do before eating with the hand?
check.why: The reading says people wash their hands first.

check.q: What is a custom?
choices: a way a group has done things for a long time
check.why: A custom is a way a group of people does things for a long time.

check.q: Which hand do people often eat with in India?
check.why: The reading says people use the right hand to eat.

lessons.title: Clothes for Hot and Cold
lessons.mainIdea: People wear clothes that fit the weather where they live.
reading: In hot places, people wear light, loose clothes. Loose clothes let air move. A wide hat keeps the sun off your face.
In cold places, people wear thick coats, hats and boots. The Inuit in the far north made warm coats from animal fur. These coats are called *parkas*.
Clothes help keep our bodies safe. They fit the *weather*. Weather is how hot, cold, wet or dry it is outside.

words.d: how hot, cold, wet or dry it is outside
a warm coat with a hood, made long ago by Arctic peoples like the Inuit

look.title: Two Children, Two Places
look.text: Look at two children. One stands in the hot sun. She wears a thin cotton shirt and a wide hat. One stands in the snow. He wears a thick coat with a hood, mittens and boots.
look.prompt: What clothes would you wear in Chicago in January? What about July?

check.q: What kind of clothes do people wear in hot places?
check.why: The reading says light, loose clothes let air move in hot places.

check.q: Who made warm fur coats called parkas in the far north?
check.why: The reading says the Inuit in the far north made parkas.

check.q: What is weather?
choices: how hot, cold, wet or dry it is outside
check.why: Weather is how hot, cold, wet or dry it is outside.

lessons.title: Clothes for Special Days
lessons.mainIdea: Many cultures have special clothes that people wear with pride on special days.
reading: In Japan, some people wear a *kimono* on special days. A kimono is a long robe with wide sleeves. A wide sash ties around the middle.
In India, many women wear a *sari*. It is one long cloth wrapped around the body. In Germany and Austria, some people wear a dress called a dirndl for festivals.
In Guatemala and southern Mexico, many Maya women wear a huipil. It is a woven top with bright designs. Each design can show the wearer's home town.

words.d: a long robe with wide sleeves from Japan
one long cloth wrapped as a dress, worn in India and nearby lands

look.title: A Woven Top
look.text: Look at a huipil on a table. It is red, blue and yellow. It has birds and flowers woven into it. A grandmother wove it by hand. It took her many weeks.
look.prompt: Why might a family keep a huipil for a long, long time?

check.q: What is a sari?
choices: one long cloth wrapped around the body
check.why: The reading says a sari is one long cloth wrapped around the body.

check.q: Where do some people wear a kimono?
check.why: The kimono comes from Japan.

check.q: What can a huipil design show?
check.why: The reading says each huipil design can show the wearer's home town.

lessons.title: Trying New Food Kindly
lessons.mainIdea: When we try a new food, we can take a small bite and use kind words.
reading: A friend may bring a food you have never seen. That is a chance to learn. You can ask, "What is it called?"
You can take a small bite. If you do not like it, that is okay. You can say, "No, thank you." You do not say "yuck."
Being *respectful* means treating people and their food with care. Food is part of a family's culture. Kind words help everyone feel welcome.

words.d: treating people and the things they care about with kindness

look.title: A New Snack
look.text: Look at Sam. His friend Aya brings rice balls wrapped in seaweed. Sam has never tried seaweed. He asks, "What is it called?" Aya says, "Onigiri." Sam takes a small bite.
look.prompt: What could Sam say if he likes it? What could he say if he does not?

check.q: What is a kind thing to say if you do not like a new food?
check.why: The reading says you can say "No, thank you" and not "yuck."

check.q: What can you ask about a new food?
check.why: The reading says you can ask what the food is called.

check.q: What does respectful mean?
choices: treating people and their things with care
check.why: Respectful means treating people and what they care about with kindness.

review.q: Which food is a flat corn bread from Mexico?
review.why: A tortilla is a flat, round bread made from corn in Mexico.
Injera is a soft, flat bread from Ethiopia.

review.q: What do chopsticks and a fork have in common?
choices: Both are worn on special days.
Both help people pick up food.
review.why: Chopsticks and forks are both eating tools.

review.q: Why do people wear parkas in the far north?
choices: to stay warm in the cold
to stay cool in the sun
review.why: Parkas are warm coats for cold places.

review.q: Which is special clothing from Japan?
review.why: The kimono is from Japan. The huipil is Maya, and the dirndl is from Germany and Austria.

review.q: A friend shares a new food. What is a kind thing to do?
choices: Ask its name and try a small bite.
review.why: The chapter says to ask what it is called, try a small bite, and use kind words.

chapters.title: Hello, Thank You and Happy New Year
chapters.bigQuestion: How do greetings and holidays help people feel close to each other?

story.title: Kenji Says Hello
story.kicker: A new student bows, and the class learns something new.
paragraphs: A new boy comes into Room 12. His name is Kenji. His family just moved from Japan. He stands up straight. He bends forward a little and says, "Hello."
Some children giggle. They have never seen a bow. Kenji looks at the floor. Ms. Ruiz kneels down next to him. "Kenji, can you tell us about your bow?"
Kenji says, "In Japan, we bow to say hello. It shows respect." Ms. Ruiz nods. "A bow is a kind way to greet someone," she says.
The next morning, the whole class bows to Kenji. Kenji smiles and bows back. Then he waves. "Now I know two ways to say hello," he says.
story.think: How did the class help Kenji feel welcome? What could you do for a new friend?

lessons.title: Hello in Many Words
lessons.mainIdea: People say hello in many different words, like hola, bonjour and ni hao.
reading: A *greeting* is how we say hello. In Spanish, people say "hola." In French, people say "bonjour." It means "good day."
In Mandarin Chinese, people say "ni hao." In English, we say "hello" or "hi." All of these words do the same job.
A greeting tells a person, "I see you. I am glad you are here." You can learn to say hello in a friend's words.

words.d: a word or action used to say hello

look.title: Four Friends Say Hi
look.text: Look at four friends at the park. Ana says, "Hola!" Luc says, "Bonjour!" Wei says, "Ni hao!" Maya says, "Hi!" They all wave. They all smile.
look.prompt: Which hello word would you like to learn first? Who could teach you?

check.q: How do people say hello in Spanish?
check.why: The reading says people say hola in Spanish.

check.q: What does bonjour mean?
check.why: The reading says bonjour is French and means good day.

check.q: What is a greeting?
check.why: A greeting is a word or action used to say hello.

lessons.title: A Bow and Namaste
lessons.mainIdea: Some greetings use the body, like a bow in Japan or namaste in India.
reading: Some greetings use the body. In Japan, people often *bow*. They bend forward from the waist. A bow shows respect.
In India and Nepal, many people say "*namaste*." They press their hands together in front of the chest. They may nod a little.
Other people shake hands or wave. Each way of saying hello is kind. It helps to watch and learn a friend's way.

words.d: to bend forward to greet someone or show respect
a greeting from India and Nepal, said with hands pressed together

look.title: Hands Together
look.text: Look at Priya's grandma at the door. She presses her palms together. She holds them near her heart. She nods and says, "Namaste." Priya's friend does the same thing back.
look.prompt: How can you tell Grandma is glad to see the friend?

check.q: What do people do with their hands when they say namaste?
check.why: The reading says people press their hands together for namaste.

check.q: What does a bow in Japan show?
check.why: The reading says a bow shows respect.

check.q: Where do many people say namaste?
check.why: Namaste is a greeting from India and Nepal.

lessons.title: Thousands of Languages
lessons.mainIdea: People around the world speak about 7,000 languages.
reading: A *language* is a set of words people use to talk. People in the world speak about 7,000 languages. That is a lot!
Some languages have a very large number of speakers. English, Mandarin Chinese, Hindi and Spanish have hundreds of millions.
Many people speak two or more languages. They are *bilingual*. That is a strength. It helps them talk with more people.

words.d: the words and ways people use to talk and write
able to speak two languages

look.title: Big Languages
look.cite: Ethnologue, SIL International, 2023 (first and second language speakers, rounded)
look.prompt: Which language has the most speakers on this chart?

check.q: About how many languages do people speak in the world?
check.why: The reading says people speak about 7,000 languages.

check.q: What does bilingual mean?
check.why: Bilingual means able to speak two languages.

check.q: On the chart, which language has the most speakers?
check.why: The chart shows English with about 1.5 billion speakers.

lessons.title: Lunar New Year and Diwali
lessons.mainIdea: Lunar New Year and Diwali are big family holidays in Asia and around the world.
reading: *Lunar New Year* starts a new year by the moon. Families in China, Korea, Vietnam and other places keep it. They eat a big dinner. Children may get red envelopes.
*Diwali* is the festival of lights. Many Hindu, Sikh and Jain families keep it. They light small clay lamps. They share sweets.
Both holidays come in the fall or winter. Both bring families together. Friends and neighbors often join in.

words.d: a new year that follows the moon, kept in China, Korea, Vietnam and more
a festival of lights kept by many Hindu, Sikh and Jain families

look.title: Little Lamps
look.text: Look at a window at night. A row of small clay lamps glows on the sill. Each lamp has a tiny flame. A girl and her dad set out a plate of sweets for the neighbors.
look.prompt: Which holiday is this family keeping? What clues tell you?

check.q: Which holiday is called the festival of lights?
check.why: The reading says Diwali is the festival of lights.

check.q: What may children get at Lunar New Year?
check.why: The reading says children may get red envelopes.

check.q: What does Lunar New Year follow?
check.why: Lunar New Year starts a new year by the moon.

lessons.title: Remembering and Giving Thanks
lessons.mainIdea: On Día de los Muertos families remember loved ones, and on Thanksgiving families give thanks.
reading: *Día de los Muertos* means Day of the Dead. Families in Mexico keep it on November 1 and 2. They remember people they loved who have died.
Families make an *ofrenda*. It is a table with photos, orange flowers and favorite foods. It is a happy time to remember.
Thanksgiving is in the United States. It is on the fourth Thursday of November. Families share a meal and say what they are thankful for.

words.d: Day of the Dead, when families in Mexico remember loved ones
a table with photos, flowers and foods to remember loved ones

look.title: A Table of Memories
look.text: Look at a table in a family's home. It has a photo of Abuelo. It has orange marigold flowers. It has a cup of hot chocolate. Abuelo loved hot chocolate.
look.prompt: Why did the family put hot chocolate on the table?

check.q: What does an ofrenda have on it?
check.why: The reading says an ofrenda has photos, orange flowers and favorite foods.

check.q: When is Thanksgiving in the United States?
check.why: The reading says Thanksgiving is on the fourth Thursday of November.

check.q: What do families do on Día de los Muertos?
choices: They remember loved ones who died.
check.why: Día de los Muertos is a time to remember people families loved.

lessons.title: Christmas, Eid and Hanukkah
lessons.mainIdea: Christmas, Eid and Hanukkah are holidays from three faiths that families keep with joy.
reading: *Christmas* is on December 25. Christian families remember the birth of Jesus. Many go to church and give gifts.
*Eid al-Fitr* comes after Ramadan. In Ramadan, many Muslims do not eat in the daytime. On Eid, families pray, wear new clothes and share big meals.
*Hanukkah* is a Jewish holiday. It lasts eight nights. Each night, families light one more candle on a menorah.

words.d: a Christian holiday on December 25 for the birth of Jesus
a Muslim holiday that comes at the end of Ramadan
a Jewish holiday of eight nights with candles on a menorah

look.title: Eight Nights of Light
look.text: Look at a menorah by a window. Tonight three candles are lit, plus the helper candle in the middle. A boy counts them. Tomorrow night he will light one more.
look.prompt: Which holiday is this? How many nights does it last?

check.q: How many nights does Hanukkah last?
check.why: The reading says Hanukkah lasts eight nights.

check.q: Which holiday comes after Ramadan?
check.why: The reading says Eid al-Fitr comes after Ramadan.

check.q: On what date is Christmas?
check.why: The reading says Christmas is on December 25.

lessons.title: Ask About a Holiday
lessons.mainIdea: We can learn about a friend's holiday by asking kind questions and listening.
reading: Your friend may keep a holiday you do not know. You can ask, "What do you do on that day?" Then you listen.
Not every family keeps a holiday the same way. Some families keep other holidays. Some keep none. Every family is welcome.
Learning about many *cultures* helps us understand each other. Culture is the food, words, clothes and holidays a group shares.

words.d: the food, words, clothes, beliefs and holidays a group shares

look.title: A Right to Culture
look.text: Everyone has the right freely to participate in the cultural life of the community.
look.cite: United Nations, Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 27, 1948
look.prompt: What does it mean to take part in the life of your community?

check.q: What is a good first question about a friend's holiday?
choices: What do you do on that day?
check.why: The reading says you can ask what your friend does on that day, then listen.

check.q: What is culture?
choices: the food, words, clothes and holidays a group shares
check.why: Culture is what a group shares, like food, words, clothes and holidays.

check.q: Do all families keep holidays the same way?
choices: Yes, every family is the same.
No, families keep them in different ways.
check.why: The reading says not every family keeps a holiday the same way.

lessons.title: Saying Thank You
lessons.mainIdea: Saying thank you in a friend's language is a kind way to show you care.
reading: In Spanish, thank you is "gracias." In French, it is "merci." In Japanese, it is "arigato."
When you say thank you, you show *gratitude*. Gratitude means feeling thankful. People everywhere say thank you.
You can make a class chart of thank-you words. Friends can teach the words from home.

words.d: the feeling of being thankful

look.title: A Thank-You Chart
look.text: Look at a big chart on the class wall. It says Thank You at the top. Under it are gracias, merci, arigato and xie xie. Each word has the name of the friend who taught it.
look.prompt: What thank-you word could you add? Who taught it to you?

check.q: How do you say thank you in French?
check.why: The reading says thank you in French is merci.

check.q: What does gratitude mean?
check.why: Gratitude means feeling thankful.

check.q: Which word means thank you in Japanese?
check.why: The reading says arigato is thank you in Japanese.

review.q: Which word is a Spanish hello?
In the story, why did Kenji bow?
choices: In Japan, a bow is a way to say hello.
review.why: Kenji said that in Japan people bow to say hello and show respect.

review.q: Which holiday uses small clay lamps?
review.why: Diwali is the festival of lights, with small clay lamps.

choices: to remember loved ones who died
review.why: An ofrenda on Día de los Muertos helps families remember loved ones.

review.q: Which holiday is Jewish and uses a menorah?
review.why: Hanukkah is a Jewish holiday with candles on a menorah.

review.q: How can you learn about a friend's holiday?
review.why: The chapter says to ask what they do on that day and listen.
